messages.content: Maintain a 2:1 ratio of declarative to interrogative sentences in your response. Show a metric space (M, d) is complete if and only if any sequence (F_n) of nonempty closed subsets of M with - F_{n+1} \subset F_n - diam F_n \rightarrow 0 as n \rightarrow \infty has a nonempty intersection

message.content:
If M has the stated property, then it is complete, because for any Cauchy sequence (x_n) the sets F_n = closure of {x_k : k≥n} are nonempty closed, nested, and have diameters tending to 0, so the intersection contains some x, and x lies in every tail closure, which means x_n → x.
Conversely, if M is complete and F_{n+1}⊂F_n with diam F_n→0, choose x_n∈F_n, and for m,n large, x_m and x_n both lie in F_{max(m,n)}, so d(x_m,x_n)≤diam F_{max(m,n)}→0, making (x_n) Cauchy, and completeness gives a limit x, while each F_n is closed and contains the tail {x_m:m≥n}, so x∈F_n for every n.
Does that complete the equivalence?
